title: Pressure and revival
hookLine: in the colonial era, monasteries lost their patrons, and lay and monastic revivals followed

cards: For a long time in Sri Lanka and Burma, the arrangement was simple. The king protected the monks, gave land to the monasteries, settled their disputes, and paid for their temples.
The monks taught, kept the texts, and blessed the kingdom. Then European empires arrived. In Sri Lanka the British took the last kingdom.
In Burma the last king was sent away into exile. The thrones that had held up the monasteries were simply gone, and new mission schools, run by Christian missionaries, became a road to a good job.
So who feeds a monastery whose patron is gone?

teach.b: First, the loss. Without kings, monasteries lost their main patrons, and the old schools in the temples lost ground to new ones run by missionaries and colonial governments.
For a while it looked, to some observers, as if the teaching might simply thin out. Second, monks turned outward.
In Sri Lanka, monks began to speak up in public: they set up printing presses, published pamphlets in the local language, and took part in open debates with Christian missionaries before crowds.
The teaching that had lived behind monastery walls came out into the town square.

teach.h: LAY PEOPLE TAKE UP THE TEXTS.
teach.b: Third, lay people took the texts into their own hands. Buddhist societies formed, raised money, and opened Buddhist schools.

In Burma, a monk named Ledi Sayadaw wrote plain manuals and taught meditation and the deeper teachings to ordinary lay people, not only to monks. Teachers who came after him carried that lay meditation far beyond Burma.
Fourth, a line that suddenly fit.

teach.h: YOU YOURSELF MUST MAKE AN EFFORT.
teach.b: The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, says: "You yourself must make an effort. The Tathâgatas (Buddhas) are only preachers."

With the kings gone, no throne was coming to hold the teaching up, so monks and lay people held it up themselves. There were hard sides to this era too: real losses, and some revivals that grew sharp and political.
But what grew out of it, Buddhist schools, lay meditation, the teaching in plain language, is still around today. Pressure, it turned out, didn't only break things. It also woke people up.

how: Buddhist societies, Sunday schools and lay meditation centers that grew out of this era still run in Sri Lanka and Myanmar, where lay people study the teachings and practice meditation alongside monks.

games.why: Ledi Sayadaw did just that: he wrote plain manuals and taught ordinary lay people, and the lay meditation that grew from it traveled far beyond Burma.

practice: Think of something that faded and came back to life because someone cared enough, a family recipe written down, a neighborhood festival restarted, a language your grandparents spoke that a cousin is learning again, and picture the people who did the work.
Hold them in mind with gratitude for a few breaths.
